beats.lead: People assume Slack was designed from day one to be workplace software.
beats.text: It was built to keep a struggling video game studio internally coordinated.
beats.note: That game was Glitch, a browser-based world from Stewart Butterfield's company, Tiny Speck.

beats.name: Glitch
beats.role: Tiny Speck's browser game — expensive to run, built on Flash just as gaming moved to mobile. Butterfield's team took its servers offline on 9 December 2012.

beats.lead: The game died. The tools built to run it didn't.
beats.text: An internal IRC-based system — channels, file sharing, searchable chat archives — became Slack's first prototype within a month of the shutdown.
beats.note: None of it was designed to be sold. It was designed to keep one struggling team talking.

beats.context: Customers Slack signed up in the first 24 hours after launching publicly in August 2013 — about a year after Glitch went dark.

beats.lead: Even the name carries a myth.
beats.text: Most people think 'Slack' is a backronym for 'Searchable Log of All Conversation and Knowledge.'
beats.note: Butterfield himself said the plain word came first, and the acronym was fitted to it afterwards.

beats.line: A dead game's leftover chat tool, now run by millions of teams that never played it.
